sections.text: Lord Shri Krishna said: He who acts because it is his duty, not thinking of the consequences, is really spiritual and a true ascetic; and not he who merely observes rituals or who shuns all action.
यं संन्यासमिति प्राहुर्योगं तं विद्धि पाण्डव।
O Arjuna! Renunciation is in fact what is called Right Action. No one can become spiritual who has not renounced all desire.
For the sage who seeks the heights of spiritual meditation, practice is the only method, and when he has attained them, he must maintain himself there by continual self-control.

We have completed chapter five. Now well be discussing chapter six. The traditional teaching says meditation is not a verb, its a noun.
It is a state to be achieved, not something you do. What you do is actually called contemplation. So what we have seen in Bhagavad Gita so far is the conclusion of the first set of chapters, and we are coming to this culminating chapter, Dhyana Yoga, which will indicate the state we have to achieve.
So we have discussed many times that Bhagavad Gita is divided into three distinct sections, each having six chapters. According to Anandagiri, who was a 13th century head of Dwarka Mutt, Bhagavad Gita is an exposition on the Mahavakya Tattvamasi. The Mahavakya is a statement which connects the lower to the higher, the jiva to the Paramatma.
Tattvamasi is a Mahavakya from the Chandogya Upanishad. Bhagavan Ved Vyas wrote Bhagavad Gita. Then Bhagavan Sankaracharya wrote a Bhasya on Bhagavad Gita, and then Anandagiri wrote a Tika on Sankaracharyas Bhasya.
There he says this Bhagavad Gita is an exposition on Tattvamasi -- that thou art. There are other opinions about what Bhagavad Gita is and how it is divided. Madhusuddhan Saraswati, a late 16th / early 17th century Advaitic scholar, said that Bhagavad Gita is divided into three parts: Karma Yoga in the first six chapters, Bhakti Yoga in chapters seven through twelve, and Gnana Yoga in chapters thirteen through eighteen. There are others who believe the first six chapters relate to the Karmakanda in the Vedas.
The next set of six chapters relates to the Upasanakanda, and the last six chapters relate to the Gnanakanda. However, Bhagavan Sankaracharya does not make any such distinction in his Bhasya. He simply says the spiritual evolution described in Bhagavad Gita follows a progression.
First, you act in this world with hankering for the fruits -- you are working with expectations. So in the first stage -- Hato va prapsyasi swargam, jitva va bhokshyase mahim -- what do you have to lose in performing any action? You shall achieve either heaven if you die, or the kingdom on this earth if you dont. When youre expecting a result, thats your motivation.
The second stage is to act without any hankering for the fruits of action, which we have seen as Karma Yoga. And then the third stage in the spiritual evolution is the integration of the mind with Upasana. The last stage, he says, is realization -- acquiring the knowledge.
So far, what we have seen is this: in chapter one, we have seen the confusion of an ordinary person of this world, which we all are. We want to act in this world and get the right results, but we do not know what actions are right. Thats our confusion.
Arjuna Vishada Yoga explained that through Arjunas condition. Chapter two gave us the philosophical perfection of the Upanishads. The highest knowledge of the Upanishads was given out right away as the goal.
Bhagavan Krishna didnt expect Arjuna to understand immediately, but he presented that knowledge of perfection -- that this self is immutable, imperishable. At the end of the chapter, we also saw the characteristics of a man of perfection, a wise person: how would he act in this world? Once you achieve the state of perfect wisdom, you will have a balanced mind. Then chapter three gave us the path of Karma Yoga, the method of self-integration of our mind and intellect.
Thats the second stage. First you act with the desire for the fruits. Then you act without desire or expectation for the fruit.
So thats chapter three. And chapter four actually gives the various means, Bahiranga, Sadhana, the external aids, how to perform Karma Yoga. So we have seen many Yajnas in chapter four.
Then chapter five gave us a technique. Even while working in this world without any expectations, there will be some impact on your mind. To avoid that, chapter five gives you the path of Renunciation: you give up the sense of agency for your actions while performing actions selflessly.
You must also renounce your sense of doership. Thats what we saw in chapter five. Renouncing the sense of agency is Sannyasa Yoga, the Yoga of Renunciation.
And now all that knowledge, if you have been practicing diligently, then Bhagavan said, you are ready for Dhyana Yoga, Yoga of Meditation. Its a yoga of contemplation. Meditation is a state to reach.
Contemplation is way to achieve that. So that is Dhyana Yoga. So you have to prepare yourself with Karma Yoga to get to Dhyana Yoga.
So the chapter literally opens with that statement. Anashritah Karmaphalam karyam karma karoti yah -- one who performs actions without depending on the fruits of actions. Sa sannyasi cha yogi cha, na niragnir na chakriyah -- such a person is a sannyasi and a yogi.
Bhagavan is now relating both yoga (which can be viewed as Karma Yoga) and sannyas as one and the same. The ultimate result is one and the same as long as you perform Karma Yoga without any expectation for the fruits. This is basically clarification.
Because we carry baggage of our culture. We see sannyasi as somebody who has given up all activities, one who is completely inactive from a societys perspective. He does not have a job, he does not have a family, he has no relationship, he has given up everything.
Sannyasi is the one who renounced everything. All means of making a living, all possessions, all relationships, including possession of his body. When somebody takes sannyas, he actually performs his own last rites.
He then wears the saffron robe. Hes not doing anything. But Bhagavan said, outwardly that person may have taken sannyas, but if he has not given up the fruits of actions, then hes not a sannyasi.
Akriyah -- he seems inactive, but that does not mean he is a sannyasi. Niragnir means one who does not have fire. This fire comes from our Vedic culture where every householder will have a fire in his house.
Because fire is necessary for your day to day cooking, but also for the religious rites. All the religious practices or upasanas were done through fire, yagnas, homas. So they used to continually keep fire in the house because they didnt have this instant matches or lighters.
So theyll keep a fire burning in the house so that when they need fire, they can use that to light bigger fire. So person who is a householder will always have fire in his house. The sannyasi gives up that responsibility of carrying fire.
He doesnt need to cook anymore, nor is he performing any religious rites or traditional pujas. Bhagavan clarifies this: a person may have given up the grihastha ashram. But if he is not at that mental level, then he is not a sannyasi.
If he has not renounced his sense of agency and the fruits of actions, then he is not a sannyasi. The clarification is that sannyasa is a state of mind -- a state of renouncing the sense of agency. The one who is a yogi is also a sannyasi; the sannyasi is also a yogi.
In the next verse, Bhagavan says: Yam sannyasam iti prahuh yogam tam viddhi Pandava -- O Pandava, that which is said to be sannyasa. Sannyasa is renouncing the sense of agency. Prahuh yogam tam viddhi Pandava -- so that sannyasa is also yoga. Because without becoming a yogi, one cannot become a sannyasi.
Na hi asannyasta sankalpah yogi bhavati kashchana -- without renouncing Sankalpa, one cannot become a yogi. Sankalpa, is a difficult word to translate in English. But expectations -- na hi asannyasta sankalpah yogi bhavati kashchana.
One who has not given up expectations cannot become a yogi. One who has not given up the fancies of the mind cannot become a yogi. Sankalpa is.
It is confusing for us because in our culture, in our vernacular languages, in our religious practices, you always do Sankalpa before you start any puja. Panditji will say, do Sankalpa. So Sankalpa also means termination, taking a vow. When I decide that this action, Im doing it for this reason, thats a sankalpa.
Im going to be regular in my exercise every day. Ill go for a walk every day as we do on a. I guess a New Years Eve, a resolution.
Because you have a goal in mind, you have a result in mind. But Bhagavan says that this Sankalpa should be given up if you want to become a yogi. Because Sankalpa is directed toward a future result, which is exactly contrary to Karma Yoga. Karma Yoga is not to expect any results.
Sankalpa is to expect a result in the future and then work towards it -- there is nothing wrong in it. But the human mind is such that Sankalpa does not remain constant. We all know that every resolution we make on New Years Eve, by the time that month is over, we have forgotten about it and moved on to some other Sankalpa.
The nature of our mind is to make a Sankalpa for the future. But the action can always be performed in present. And before we start that action in present, we move on to the next Sankalpa.
We want to do something else. So we never reach a goal. Because the goal is constantly a moving target that the fancy of our mind.
So to stop that one has to give up Sankalpa. One has to learn how to give up this fancy of a mind. And I heard that you have to learn how to give up Sankalpa to get Sankalpa Siddhi.
Sankalpa Siddhi means youre determined to get something, you work towards it, and you get it. So if you make a Sankalpa for something unattainable -- like Moksha, liberation -- then first you have to learn how to give up the other fancies of your mind. Give up all the other fleeting Sankalpas and just work toward that one Sankalpa of liberation.
Then you can reach that. So learn how to give up minor Sankalpas so you can achieve Sankalpa Siddhi for the ultimate goal. Bhagavan here says that no one can become a yogi who has not given up Sankalpa.
He is already a renouncer. He has given up Sankalpa. He is a sannyasi and therefore he is a yogi.
So yogi and sannyasi are one and the same. Then the Gita tells us who should practice what -- who is capable of inactivity and who should perform actions. We have already seen that inactivity is not an option for us.
Its not possible for any living being to be inactive. But inactivity is the goal. We want Nishkarma Siddhi -- we want to retire from our day-to-day pursuits.
So he says: Arurukshoh muner yogam karma karanam uchyate -- Karma is the means for a seeker, a muni who wants to ascend to yoga, who wants to become a yogi but is not a yogi yet. The one who has control over his mind is a yogi. For one who wants to control his mind but whose mind is not yet in control, Karma is prescribed.
Remember, we have started a chapter called Dhyana Yoga. So we expected that Bhagavan would just talk about Dhyana -- how to meditate, what to do. We thought we were done with Karma Yoga.
Now lets focus on Dhyana Yoga. But Bhagavan really puts Karma Yoga at the highest level here and say unless you have practiced Karma Yoga and achieved the results of the Karma Yoga which is the control of the mind, purification of the mind, the next step is not really for you.

These opening verses of Dhyana Yoga reveal a profound truth: true renunciation is not about giving up external activities, but about releasing our grip on expected outcomes. As Krishna declares, Anashritah karmaphalam karyam karma karoti yah - one who performs obligatory actions without depending on the fruits is both a sannyasi and a yogi. This challenges our conventional understanding of spiritual practice. We often believe we must retreat from life to find inner peace, but the Gita insists that real yoga happens in the midst of action, when we learn to work without the anxiety of results.
Consider your own relationship with Sankalpa - those overarching desires and resolutions that constantly shift and change in your mind. How many New Years resolutions have faded by February? The teaching here is not to eliminate all goals, but to recognize when your fanciful mind is creating endless moving targets that keep you perpetually chasing rather than arriving. Today, examine one activity you perform regularly. Can you do it with full attention and care, yet without mentally leaping ahead to what you hope to gain from it? Notice how giving up expectation paradoxically brings more peace to the action itself.
Ask yourself: Am I still climbing the ladder of yoga (arurukshu), requiring the discipline of Karma Yoga? Or have I reached a place of inner stillness (yoga-rudha) where the mind naturally rests? Be honest - most of us are still climbing, and that is exactly where we should be applying selfless action as our practice.
